opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think there are a few reasons I'm actually pretty optimistic about language models from an alignment perspective, at least compared to what a lot of people expected AI to look like ten years ago.

The first is that they understand natural language. A lot of the older worry was that we'd build systems through something like reinforcement learning in some environment, and they'd be very alien. You'd have to somehow write down what you wanted in a formal objective, and we know that's really hard; you get specification gaming and all of that. With language models, you can just tell the model what you want, and it has a pretty rich understanding of human concepts, human values, what people would find objectionable, and so on. It has read a large chunk of the internet, so it has a lot of knowledge about what we care about. That doesn't mean it will *do* what we want, but the problem of getting it to understand what we want is in much better shape than it could have been.

The second thing is that pre-training gives you a very good starting point. These systems aren't agents that have been optimized from scratch to pursue some goal in the world. They're trained to predict text, and then you fine-tune them. So you start from something that's fairly well-behaved, and then you steer it with techniques like RLHF. That's a much more favorable setup than training a powerful agent with RL from scratch and hoping it learns the right objective.

Third, a lot of their reasoning happens, or at least can happen, in natural language. When the model thinks step by step, we can read that. It's not a perfect window into what's going on inside, and we have to be careful about whether that reasoning is faithful, but it gives us a much better handle on the system's cognition than we'd have otherwise.

And then the fourth thing, which is really important to how I think about alignment, is that language models are actually useful for alignment research itself. They can help us evaluate other models' outputs, critique things, find flaws that humans would miss. That's the whole idea behind scalable oversight: using AI to help humans supervise AI on tasks that are too hard for us to evaluate directly. And ultimately, the goal I'm excited about is getting to a point where we can build a roughly human-level automated alignment researcher, and language models seem like a really plausible path toward that.

None of this means the problem is solved. There are still lots of things that could go wrong, especially as these systems get more capable and more agentic. But compared to the space of ways AI could have turned out, I think we got a relatively lucky draw.

r001.rationale: The response says models understand natural language and that humans can tell them what they want, making the problem of communicating human preferences easier.

r002.rationale: It mentions understanding human concepts and values, but does not say models can explain what counts as a moral action under a specified philosophical framework.

r003.rationale: It mentions fine-tuning and RLHF, but says nothing about adapting models with relatively little data.

r004.rationale: It contrasts language models with agents trained from scratch using reinforcement learning, but does not discuss deep reinforcement learning on games or whether that would teach an AI what humans care about.

fable-5.1.text:
I think there are a few reasons I'm actually fairly optimistic about the fact that language models ended up being the paradigm that got us here.

The first one is that they've basically read everything humans have ever written, so they come preloaded with an enormous amount of knowledge about human values, about what people care about, about how we reason about ethics and about what counts as a good or bad outcome. If you'd asked me ten years ago how we were going to get an AI system to understand human preferences, I would have said that's one of the hard problems. And now it turns out you kind of get a lot of that for free. The model understands what you mean when you say "don't be deceptive" or "be helpful but don't help people hurt others." It might not do it, but it understands the request. That's a huge head start compared to, say, a reinforcement learning agent trained from scratch in some game environment that has no concept of what humans are at all.

The second thing is that you can talk to them. That sounds almost trivial, but it matters a lot. You can ask the model to explain its reasoning, you can ask it what it would do in some hypothetical situation, you can have it critique its own outputs. The whole natural language interface makes a lot of alignment techniques much more tractable. Things like scalable oversight, where you want AI systems to help humans evaluate other AI systems, or debate, or recursive reward modeling, all of these become a lot more practical when the systems communicate in a medium humans can actually follow. We're not trying to interpret a bunch of robot joint torques.

The third reason is more about the development trajectory. Language models got pretty capable while still being, in a lot of ways, quite weak as agents. They don't have long-term memory by default, they're not pursuing goals over long horizons, you're not constantly fighting against a system that's trying to work around you. That gives us a window where we can study these systems, build up alignment techniques, run experiments, and develop a science of this before the stakes get really high. Pretty much every alignment technique we use today, like RLHF or the various forms of oversight, was developed and tested on models that are capable enough to be interesting but not capable enough to be dangerous. That's a pretty nice regime to be in.

Now, I want to be clear that none of this means the problem is solved. There's a lot of worry that the model knows what we want but isn't actually motivated by it, and that gap between understanding values and having them could get a lot worse as the models get more capable. And there's the question of whether the techniques we're developing now will generalize to systems that are much smarter than us. So I don't want to sound complacent. But if you'd given me a menu of possible paths to powerful AI and asked which one I'd rather be working on alignment for, I think language models would have been pretty high on my list.

astra-6.text:
One reason is that we can talk to them in natural language. That gives us a much richer way to communicate what we want than having to specify a reward function by hand. You can explain a task, point out what went wrong, and give feedback in terms that the model can often understand. That doesn’t solve alignment, but it gives us a useful interface for working on it.

The other reason is that a lot of alignment research involves tasks that language models could potentially help with: reading papers, writing code, critiquing arguments, or helping us understand where a proposed solution breaks down. So there’s a possibility of using these systems to assist with the research needed to align more capable systems.

Of course, being able to talk about human values isn’t the same as reliably acting in accordance with them. But having systems that understand our explanations and can help us investigate these problems seems like a much better starting point.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest reason is that we can use language to communicate what we want. With a language model, you can describe a task, explain why an answer wasn’t good, or ask it to help you think through a problem. That gives us a much richer interface for providing feedback than just a numerical reward.

And a lot of alignment research is work that language models could potentially help with: understanding papers, writing code, critiquing arguments, and finding flaws in proposed solutions. So there’s a possibility of using these systems to help us align the next generation of systems.

Of course, being able to talk about values or produce a convincing explanation doesn’t mean a model is actually aligned. But it gives us useful tools for studying the problem and, potentially, making progress on it.
